PHSCS 587

PN depletion electrostatics

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how unequal depleted widths balance equal and opposite charge

Joining p-type and n-type material creates concentration gradients. Initial diffusion uncovers negative ionized acceptors on the p side and positive ionized donors on the n side. Their electric field points from n toward p and opposes further majority-carrier diffusion. At equilibrium a common Fermi level and balanced drift and diffusion accompany this built-in field.

For an abrupt junction in the depletion approximation, mobile charge is neglected inside widths xp and xn. Charge neutrality per area requires NAxp = NDxn. The total depleted width is W = xp + xn = √{[2εs(Vbi − V)/q](1/NA + 1/ND)}, where εs is semiconductor permittivity, V is positive for forward bias, and Vbi is the equilibrium built-in potential. Width and concentration units must be consistent.

For fully ionized nondegenerate uniform sides, Vbi = VT ln(NAND/ni²). Forward bias reduces the depletion potential Vbi − V; reverse bias increases it. The approximation applies while a depleted region exists and effects such as high injection, tunneling, breakdown and strong grading can be neglected. The less heavily doped side occupies more of W.

Example

If NA = 4ND, charge balance gives xn = 4xp: the more lightly doped n side has four times the depleted width. At fixed doping, doubling the depletion potential increases W by √2.

Practice

1. Why does a built-in field coexist with zero net equilibrium current?

Count both drift and diffusion.

The field-driven current balances the concentration-gradient-driven current for each carrier type at thermal equilibrium.

2. Which side holds most of the depletion width in a strongly one-sided junction?

Use NAxp = NDxn.

The lower-doped side needs a larger width to supply the same magnitude of uncovered ion charge.
